data.title: Middle East Eye: Gaza declares meningitis alert as health ministry blames Israeli restrictions
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Gaza declares meningitis alert as health ministry blames Israeli restrictions
Gaza’s health ministry has issued an “epidemiological alert” across the territory, warning that a “shocking” increase in meningitis infections puts hundreds of thousands of lives at risk, particularly children.
The ministry urged the World Health Organization and Unicef to launch an emergency response.
Dr Nidal Ghunaim, deputy director general of primary healthcare for public health, reported 272 cases in October. He described the figure as more than eight times the usual monthly average of 30 to 50.
Meningitis has killed 15 people this year, Ghunaim said, including five during the August-to-October surge.
The ministry described the outbreak as an “inevitable result of the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowding of shelters, mixing of drinking water with sewage, and the disaster being exacerbated by flooding due to rain”.
“We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak due to its prevention of the entry of maintenance spare parts, sterilization materials and fuel,” it said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: How EU failure to regulate tech made Palestine a ‘laboratory’ for AI weaponry and surveillance
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
How EU failure to regulate tech made Palestine a ‘laboratory’ for AI weaponry and surveillance
This week, the Geneva Convention held its Seventh Review Conference on the development of technological warfare and its humanitarian implications.
The review takes place every five years and aims to negotiate legally binding international agreements on restricting autonomous weapon systems, amid growing concerns over their use against civilians. However, powerful militarised countries like the US and Russia generally block progress.
Since the last review, the use of AI-powered weapons has accelerated exponentially, with much of the cutting-edge technology being used by Israelis against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank by Israel.
Despite this, Palestine was barely mentioned during the UN meeting.
Last week, the Palestinian digital rights organisation 7amleh organised a conference in Brussels, attended by Middle East Eye, bringing together policymakers, journalists, politicians and researchers to assess the use of autonomous weapons in the context of the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Rohingya genocide case: How The Gambia went to The Hague and won
data.author: Sondos Asem
data.summary:
Rohingya genocide case: How The Gambia went to The Hague and won
Submitted by
Sondos Asem
on
Sun, 11/22/2026 - 15:04
Lead counsel Arsalan Suleman tells Middle East Eye how the small African country took Myanmar to court and how survivor testimony helped secure a landmark judgement
Eighty years after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) first sat in The Hague, I walked into the Peace Palace’s Great Hall of Justice to photograph the judges as they took their seats.
They were about to deliver a landmark judgment in a trailblazing case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar. For the first time, the court would find that a state had committed genocide, the "crime of all crimes" as it has been described.
It had been seven years since The Gambia, a slither of a country of less than three million people in West Africa that is named after the river that dissects it, filed the case.
It argued that Myanmar was trying to destroy the Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority that has lived in Rakhine State on the country's western coast for generations.
The case was brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the UN’s first human rights treaty, drawn up in the wake of the Holocaust to define genocide under international law and require states to prevent and punish it.
In the past, international criminal tribunals have convicted individuals of genocide, such as in courts created to prosecute atrocities committed during the wars in the former Yugoslavia and in Rwanda in the 1990s.
But this time the question before the ICJ, the UN’s highest court which adjudicates mainly in disputes between states, was whether Myanmar itself, as a state actor, can be held responsible.
In 2017, Myanmar’s military burned Rohingya villages, carried out mass killings and widespread rape, and deliberately killed children, the court found. Soldiers shot civilians as they fled, including people trying to swim to safety.

Yemen’s Houthi-run Economy Ministry says Saudi attacks and the blockade have inflicted more than $1.13 trillion in cumulative economic losses since the war began began in March 2015.
Acting Economy Minister Sam al-Bashiri said preliminary estimates put direct damage during the latest escalation, from 13 July to 23 November, at more than $881.5m, Saba reports.
He said Saudi strikes destroyed 22 factories and partially damaged three others, causing industrial losses exceeding $376m.
The ministry put commercial losses above $85m and investment-sector losses above $20m.
Transport and Public Works Minister Mohammed Quhaim reported more than $350m in damage to infrastructure and other sectors during the same period.
Quhaim said attacks on airports, ports, roads and bridges had disrupted supplies and increased shipping, insurance and storage costs, placing further financial pressure on Yemenis.

The Canadian judge said one transfer was a wedding gift for a young couple and the other was a hotel payment. Both were sent from the Netherlands in euros to Britain in pounds. A US bank’s UK branch became involved in both transactions, she said.
“In the United Kingdom, I have two instances where money was blocked and remains frozen,” Prost told journalists at the court’s headquarters in The Hague.
“And this is the scenario, money sent from here in the Netherlands in euros to the United Kingdom in pounds, and I get an email which says: ‘Your money has been blocked on the basis of the order of the President of the United States, and if you want your money back, you must apply to the Office of Foreign Assets Control in the United States for a licence.’”
In response to a request for comment, the UK foreign office did not address Prost's concerns. Instead, a source said that the UK "stands with the ICC" and is opposed to the sanctions.
Her account sheds light on the personal toll of crippling US sanctions ahead of the ICC’s annual Assembly of States Parties, which opens in The Hague on 30 November.

data.summary:
Saudi finance minister claims kingdom can withstand prolonged Houthi conflict
Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed al-Jadaan says the kingdom is “resilient enough to withstand a prolonged conflict” with Yemen’s Houthis.
Speaking to reporters, al-Jadaan dismissed as “a total mistake” any expectation that attacks on civilian infrastructure or “blackmail by missiles” would force Riyadh to compromise its national security.
He said Saudi Arabia plans to reduce its budget deficit to 3.6 percent of GDP in 2027, compared with an estimated 4.9 percent this year, despite the escalating fighting.
The Iran-backed Houthis say their missile and drone campaign aims to force Riyadh to withdraw support for Yemen’s government.
Al-Jadaan said reduced oil production had driven a 2.1 percent contraction in Saudi GDP this year.

On Sunday, fraught global climate talks in Turkey, the longest ever in the climate conference’s history, ground to a halt, with no deal. The EU, UK and allies rejected the draft text over its failure to mention fossil fuels.
At the closing plenary, Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien, on behalf of the EU, rejected the text, saying it “does not respond to the science, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required… that does not even mention fossil fuels”.
His words were met with applause. But they rang hollow for developing countries, many of whom also rejected the text over its weak language on climate finance.
After delivering his intervention, O’Brien and EU Climate Minister Wopke Hoekstra walked out of the plenary to hold a press huddle while developing nations were speaking about the need for climate finance.
